name: Reverse wrist curl
angleNote: Wrist extension: 0° = hand in line with the forearm, negative = curled down towards the palm (stretched), positive = bent back. Elbow at the origin.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The hand's centre of mass is given along wrist → third knuckle; here it is applied along wrist → grip, which is about as long.
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Elbow→wrist and wrist→grip centre in metres, typical adult. Estimates (TODO: anthropometric source).

strengthCurve.label: Wrist extensor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric wrist-extension moment vs wrist angle (positive = bent back, negative = curled): nearly flat, strongest with the wrist bent back about 20°, three quarters of that curled 60°. Average curve of 10 men (negated angles of their figure), forearm supinated, elbow at 90°. Peak torque default 6.5 Nm: the average curve's peak (individual peaks averaged 7.1 Nm, about 60% of flexion).
strengthCurve.source: Delp SL, Grierson AE, Buchanan TS (1996). Maximum isometric moments generated by the wrist muscles in flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation. J Biomech 29(10):1371–1375. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(96)00029-2 (Fig. 2, read off; 10 men, forearm supinated, elbow at 90°)

weightsNote: Muscle weights (extensors): each muscle's moment-generating potential, PCSA × wrist moment arm, relative to the largest at that wrist angle; held flat outside the two angles given. If the load is shared to keep the summed squared activation smallest, activation scales with this potential, so the bars show that pattern, not EMG. The finger flexors are included because they cross the wrist: Gonzalez et al. found they supply about 68% of the flexion potential at 40° of flexion (the long finger and wrist extensors about 45% and 55% of the extension potential).
weightsSource: Gonzalez RV, Buchanan TS, Delp SL (1997). How muscle architecture and moment arms affect wrist flexion-extension moments. J Biomech 30(7):705–712. doi:10.1016/S0021-9290(97)00015-8 (Table 1: PCSA × moment arm at neutral, at 40° of flexion for the flexors and 20° of extension for the extensors)

muscles.name: Extensor carpi radialis brevis
muscles.note: Main wrist extensor; its origin at the elbow is the usual site of tennis elbow.

muscles.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus
muscles.note: Wrist extensor on the thumb side; also a weak elbow flexor.

muscles.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
muscles.note: Wrist extensor on the little-finger side.

muscles.name: Extensor digitorum
muscles.note: Finger extensor that also crosses the wrist; as big a contributor as the ECRB.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Wrist curled down, extensors stretched. The weight hangs below the hand's line, so the moment arm is shrinking.

phases.name: Middle
phases.text: Hand in line with the forearm: the weight is furthest from the wrist horizontally, the hardest point.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Wrist bent back. The weight moves over the wrist and gets easier, while the extensors get weaker as they shorten.

variants.name: Seated reverse wrist curl (dumbbell, palm down)
variants.notes: Forearm flat on the thigh, palm down. Torque ∝ cos(wrist angle), like the palm-up curl, but the extensors are much weaker than the flexors, so the same dumbbell feels far heavier.

variants.name: Cable reverse wrist curl (low pulley)
variants.notes: Palm down, cable from a low pulley in front of the hand: more tension at the top than with a dumbbell. Move the pulley to see the peak shift.
